newsitem.title: USA: Soybean, wheat prices jump on strong exports.
newsitem.headline: Soybean, wheat prices jump on strong exports.

text.p: Soybean and wheat prices jumped Thursday, helped by strong exports and a government report showing soybean stockpiles were shrinking.
In other markets, oil prices rebounded from this week's steep declines, as an outage at a East Coast refinery threatened to pinch supplies of gasoline in the Northeast.
In the grain market, traders noted that weekly soybean exports were as much as 40 percent higher than expected just as it became apparent that stockpiles will not be as large.
The Agriculture Department estimated that soybean stockpiles will fall to 180 million bushels as of Aug. 31, 1997, from 210 million bushels estimated last month.
The difference was higher projected exports. The government raised its estimate of the corn "carryover" slightly to 1.16 billion bushels.
"The supply (and) demand (report) was a surprise for soybeans. The fact they increased exports 30 million bushels was a surprise," Steve Bruce of E.D. and F. Man International said.
"The technical picture looks better and the fundamental news was supportive," Ron Kucha of O'Connor and Co. added.
Soybeans for January delivery jumped 11.25 cents to $7.02-3/4 a bushel at the Chicago Board of Trade.
Wheat prices gained after India said it will import much more wheat than had been expected to bolster stockpiles and check rising prices.

Food Minister Devendra Prasad Yadav told India's parliament the country will import 2 million metric tons of wheat this year, double what many analysts had predicted. While most of the wheat will probably come from Australia and other suppliers, it will boost global demand.
December wheat gained 5 cents to $4.04 a bushel, while December corn edged up 0.25 cent to $2.67-3/4 a bushel.
Bruce of E.D. and F. Man said higher livestock prices boded well for corn prices, since ranchers will rebuild herds and increase demand for feed corn.
Oil prices recovered part of this week's steep drop, aided by higher gasoline prices.
An outage at a gasoline unit at Tosco Corp.'s huge New Jersey refinery, a major supplier to the Northeast, helped push prices higher.

But traders said other factors may have outweighed the outage at the Tosco refinery. Energy Department figures issued earlier this week showed U.S. refiners produced at near-record levels and there was a big influx of imports expected this month.
January gasoline rose 1.16 cents to 64.72 cents a gallon at the New York Mercantile Exchange. January crude oil added 34 cents to $23.72 a barrel after falling more than $2 earlier this week.
"Crude oil has spent the day nursing the hangover acquired in dropping $2 in two days," said Tim Evans, an energy analyst at Pegasus Econometrics in New York.
Oil prices had dropped after Iraq resumed exporting following a six-year hiatus.
